# Tutorial 02: The Geometry of Cash Flows

## Exercise 1: Grandma's Study Grant

Max's grandmother wants to support his four-year bachelor's programme with **€2,400 per year**. Being a woman of principle, she lets Max choose only the *timing*: either at the **end** of each study year or at the **start** of each study year (first payment today). Max could invest any money he receives at **3% p.a.**

#### Task 1: Present value of both options

a) Place both payment streams on a timeline ($t = 0$ to $t = 4$).

b) Calculate the present value of both options. Which one should Max choose, and by how much is it worth more?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Given: $C = 2{,}400$; $i = 3\%$; $n = 4$.

**a)** Timeline (payments in €):

| $t$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|:----|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| End of year (ordinary annuity) | — | 2,400 | 2,400 | 2,400 | 2,400 |
| Start of year (annuity due) | 2,400 | 2,400 | 2,400 | 2,400 | — |

**b)** Ordinary annuity:

$$PVIFA(3\%,\,4) = \frac{1.03^4 - 1}{0.03 \cdot 1.03^4} = 3.7171 \qquad PV_{\text{ord}} = 2{,}400 \cdot 3.7171 = 8{,}921.04$$

Annuity due:

$$PV_{\text{due}} = 8{,}921.04 \cdot 1.03 = 9{,}188.67$$

Max should choose the **start-of-year payments**; they are worth **€267.63 more** today (exactly 3% of €8,921.04). Same four payments, same total of €9,600 — only the timing differs.

**Grading Notes:** The table value 3.7171 gives the same result, €8,921.04. Full marks for b) require the factor $(1+i)$ or an equivalent argument (one undiscounted payment today plus three discounted ones).
:::

#### Task 2: Future value at graduation

Instead of paying Max directly, grandmother deposits each instalment in a savings account at 3% and hands Max the balance at the end of year 4. How much will he receive under each timing option? How much of it is interest?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Ordinary annuity — value at $t = 4$, immediately after the last deposit:

$$FV_{\text{ord}} = 2{,}400 \cdot \frac{1.03^4 - 1}{0.03} = 2{,}400 \cdot 4.183627 = 10{,}040.70$$

Annuity due — every deposit earns one more year of interest:

$$FV_{\text{due}} = 10{,}040.70 \cdot 1.03 = 10{,}341.93$$

Interest: $10{,}040.70 - 9{,}600 = 440.70$ (ordinary) and $10{,}341.93 - 9{,}600 = 741.93$ (annuity due).

Alternative route: compound the present values from Task 1 forward, $8{,}921.04 \cdot 1.03^4 \approx 10{,}040.71$ (one cent rounding difference) and $9{,}188.67 \cdot 1.03^4 = 10{,}341.93$. The future value of an annuity is its present value moved to the right on the timeline.
:::

## Exercise 2: From Lump Sum to Instalment

Three small decisions, one tool: the Capital Recovery Factor. All payments are made at the **end** of each year unless stated otherwise.

#### Task 1: The café loan

Defne opens a specialty café and borrows **€35,000** at **7% p.a.**, repayable in **six equal annual instalments**.

a) Calculate the annual instalment.

b) How much of the first instalment is interest, and how much repays the loan?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Given: $PV = 35{,}000$; $i = 7\%$; $n = 6$.

**a)**

$$C = 35{,}000 \cdot CRF(7\%,\,6) = 35{,}000 \cdot \frac{0.07 \cdot 1.07^6}{1.07^6 - 1} = 35{,}000 \cdot 0.209796 = 7{,}342.85$$

(With the table value 0.2098: €7,343.00.)

**b)** Interest in year 1 is charged on the full loan: $35{,}000 \cdot 0.07 = 2{,}450.00$. The rest repays the loan: $7{,}342.85 - 2{,}450.00 = 4{,}892.85$. (The full repayment schedule follows in Chapter 3.)
:::

#### Task 2: Saving for a down payment

Paul wants to have **€25,000** for the down payment on a flat in **five years**. He saves an equal amount at the end of each year in an account paying **4% p.a.** How much must he save per year, and how much of the €25,000 will be interest?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Given: $FV = 25{,}000$; $i = 4\%$; $n = 5$.

**Route 1 — future value of an annuity set equal to the target:**

$$25{,}000 = C \cdot \frac{1.04^5 - 1}{0.04} = C \cdot 5.416323 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad C = 4{,}615.68$$

**Route 2 — discount the target, then apply the CRF:**

$$PV = 25{,}000 \cdot 1.04^{-5} = 20{,}548.18 \qquad C = 20{,}548.18 \cdot CRF(4\%,\,5) = 20{,}548.18 \cdot 0.224627 = 4{,}615.68$$

(With the table value 0.2246: €4,615.12.) Paul saves $5 \cdot 4{,}615.68 = 23{,}078.39$ himself; interest contributes $25{,}000 - 23{,}078.39 = 1{,}921.61$.

**Grading Notes:** Either route earns full marks. A common error is $25{,}000 \cdot CRF(4\%,\,5)$ without discounting — this treats the target as a value *today* and gives €5,615.68.
:::

#### Task 3: How much loan can I afford?

Lukas can spend at most **€9,000 per year** on loan instalments. His bank offers **5% p.a.** over **8 years**.

a) What is the largest loan he can take out?

b) The bank offers to stretch the term to **10 years** at the same rate. How much more could he borrow?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Here the instalment is given and the lump sum is sought — the PVIFA direction.

**a)**

$$PV = 9{,}000 \cdot PVIFA(5\%,\,8) = 9{,}000 \cdot 6.463213 = 58{,}168.91$$

(With the table value 6.4632: €58,168.80.)

**b)**

$$PV = 9{,}000 \cdot PVIFA(5\%,\,10) = 9{,}000 \cdot 7.721735 = 69{,}495.61$$

Lukas could borrow $69{,}495.61 - 58{,}168.91 = 11{,}326.70$ more — at the price of two additional years of payments.
:::

## Exercise 3: Forever and Ever

The Erlenbach parish owns a plot of land and has granted a company a ground lease (dt. *Erbbaurecht*) that, for the purpose of this exercise, runs **forever**. The ground rent is **€18,000 per year**; the parish values the income at **4.5% p.a.**

#### Task 1: Constant perpetuity

a) What is the ground lease worth to the parish if the rent is paid at the end of each year (first payment in one year)?

b) What is it worth if the rent is paid in advance, with the first payment today?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

**a)**

$$PV = \frac{C}{i} = \frac{18{,}000}{0.045} = 400{,}000$$

**b)** One payment today plus the perpetuity from a):

$$PV = 18{,}000 + 400{,}000 = 418{,}000 \qquad \text{(equivalently } 400{,}000 \cdot 1.045 = 418{,}000\text{)}$$
:::

#### Task 2: Indexed rent

The lease contract contains an index clause: the ground rent rises by **1.5% p.a.** forever.

a) Value the lease if the **next** payment (in one year) is €18,000.

b) Value the lease if the rent paid **this year** was €18,000, so that the next payment is already indexed.

c) A board member proposes to assume a growth rate of 4.5%, "to be on the safe side". What happens?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

**a)** Growing perpetuity with $C_1 = 18{,}000$, $g = 1.5\% < i = 4.5\%$:

$$PV = \frac{18{,}000}{0.045 - 0.015} = \frac{18{,}000}{0.03} = 600{,}000$$

**b)** Now the first future payment is $C_1 = 18{,}000 \cdot 1.015 = 18{,}270$:

$$PV = \frac{18{,}270}{0.03} = 609{,}000$$

**c)** With $g = i = 4.5\%$ the denominator is zero. Every payment then has the same present value, and infinitely many of them add up to infinity — the growing-perpetuity formula does not apply. "Safe side" is the wrong label: a higher growth rate makes the valuation *more* optimistic, and at $g \geq i$ no finite value exists.

**Grading Notes:** b) tests the definition of $C_1$ as the payment one period from now. Using €18,000 in b) is the classic error.
:::

#### Task 3: A perpetuity that starts later

The municipality promises the local sports club a grant of **€5,000 per year forever**, but the first payment will only be made at the end of **year 5**. What is the promise worth today at **4% p.a.**?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

**Step 1 — perpetuity formula.** $C/i$ delivers the value one period *before* the first payment, i.e. at $t = 4$:

$$PV_4 = \frac{5{,}000}{0.04} = 125{,}000$$

**Step 2 — discount to today** (Chapter 1):

$$PV_0 = 125{,}000 \cdot 1.04^{-4} = 125{,}000 \cdot 0.854804 = 106{,}850.52$$

**Grading Notes:** Discounting over five instead of four periods (result €102,740.89) is the typical timeline error; award partial credit for the correct Step 1.
:::

## Exercise 4: Concepts and Transfer

#### Task 1: Multiple choice — factors and formulas

Which of the following statements are **correct**? (Multiple answers possible.)

a) The Capital Recovery Factor is the reciprocal of the PVIFA.

b) For $i > 0$, $PVIFA(i,\,n)$ is always smaller than $n$.

c) The present value of an annuity due is lower than that of an ordinary annuity with the same payments, because it ends one period earlier.

d) The perpetuity formula $C/i$ gives the value one period before the first payment.

e) A growing perpetuity with $g = i$ is worth $C_1/(1+i)$.

f) $CRF(5\%,\,10) = 0.10$, because the loan is repaid in ten equal parts.

g) All statements are false.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:** Correct are **a)**, **b)** and **d)**.

- **a) Correct.** $CRF(i,\,n) = 1/PVIFA(i,\,n)$.
- **b) Correct.** Each of the $n$ discount factors is below 1, so their sum is below $n$ (e.g. $PVIFA(5\%,\,10) = 7.7217 < 10$).
- **c) Incorrect.** Every payment of an annuity due arrives one period *earlier*, so its present value is *higher* by the factor $(1+i)$.
- **d) Correct.** That is why a perpetuity starting later must be discounted from one period before its first payment (Exercise 3, Task 3).
- **e) Incorrect.** $C_1/(1+i)$ is the present value of *each* payment; infinitely many of them sum to infinity — no finite value exists.
- **f) Incorrect.** $CRF(5\%,\,10) = 0.1295$. The instalment must cover interest as well as repayment, so the CRF always exceeds $1/n$.
- **g) Incorrect**, since a), b) and d) are correct.
:::

#### Task 2: Transfer — how much is "forever" worth?

A municipal utility values its district-heating network as a growing perpetuity: expected cash flow next year **€2 million**, discount rate **6%**, growth rate **5%**. A sceptical council member argues that 4% growth is more realistic.

a) Calculate the value under both growth assumptions.

b) Explain in three to four sentences why such a small change in $g$ has such a large effect, and what this means for how much trust the council should place in the valuation.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

**a)**

$$PV_{g = 5\%} = \frac{2{,}000{,}000}{0.06 - 0.05} = 200{,}000{,}000 \qquad PV_{g = 4\%} = \frac{2{,}000{,}000}{0.06 - 0.04} = 100{,}000{,}000$$

Lowering growth by one percentage point **halves** the value from €200 million to €100 million.

**b)** The value depends on the *difference* $i - g$, not on $i$ and $g$ separately. When $g$ is close to $i$, that difference is tiny, so a change of one percentage point in $g$ changes the denominator by 50% or 100% — and the value by the same proportion. The growth rate is also the hardest input to verify, because it is assumed to hold forever. The council should therefore treat a growing-perpetuity value with $g$ close to $i$ as a range rather than a number, test several growth rates, and ask whether a growth rate this close to the discount rate is plausible for an asset that grows with the local economy.

**Grading Notes:** Full marks require the link between $i - g$ and sensitivity, plus a judgement on reliability. Accept the observation that at $g = 5.5\%$ the value would double again to €400 million.
:::
